report.tagline: A UK gym-clothing brand that grew from a garage to a global name by building a community of fitness influencers instead of buying ads.
report.simpleSummary: Gymshark makes leggings, shorts, sports bras and hoodies for people who work out. It started in 2012 when Ben Francis, then 19, sewed and screen-printed clothes in his parents' garage in Birmingham. It grew by sending clothes to fitness YouTubers and Instagram stars, whose fans wanted to look like them. It sells mainly through its own website and app, and now has shops like its Regent Street flagship in London.

overview.whatItDoes: Gymshark designs gym clothes and sells them mostly direct to customers online, without department stores in the middle. Its marketing runs on 'Gymshark Athletes', a roster of fitness creators who wear the clothes and post workouts. It has opened its own stores and a training app to deepen the community.
howItWorks: Gymshark designs ranges like Vital Seamless and Adapt leggings in Solihull, England, and has them made by partner factories.
Most sales happen on gymshark.com and the app, in collection 'drops' that create urgency.
Gymshark Athletes, paid fitness creators, wear the kit in workout videos and on Instagram and TikTok.
The free Gymshark Training app offers workout plans, tying the brand to the actual workout.
Own stores, such as Regent Street in London and newer US locations, double as community spaces with events and runs.
Discounts are mostly kept to big events like Black Friday, to protect the brand's full-price image.
overview.valueProposition: Gym clothes that look and feel good, made for real workouts, at prices below Lululemon, from a brand that feels like part of the fitness scene you follow online.

userJourneys.name: First purchase after a creator video

Taps the link in bio to gymshark.com.
Checks the size guide and reviews on fit.
Pays about £45 with Klarna or a card.
Wears it to the gym and posts a mirror photo, tagging the brand.
Downloads the Gymshark Training app from a prompt in the email.
Gets an app alert that a new collection drops at 6pm.
Rushes to buy before sizes sell out.
Waits for shipping during a busy period.
Posts the new kit on Instagram.
Walks past the Regent Street store.
Signs up for a community run.
Buys in store or orders a missing size online.
Joins the email list for future drops.

businessModel.summary: Gymshark makes clothes and sells most of them directly to customers, keeping the margin a wholesaler or shop would take. It spends on creators, events and stores instead of TV ads. Profit has dropped as it invests in stores, the US and new teams.

revenueStreams.detail: The website and app make up most of revenue.
Flagships in London and newer US stores.
Small partnerships with selected retailers in some markets.

businessModel.pricing: Leggings around £40 to £55, sports bras around £30 to £40, hoodies around £45 to £60 in the UK. Free delivery over a minimum order in many markets. Discounts mostly at Black Friday and seasonal sales.
costDrivers: Payments to Gymshark Athletes and creators
Store rent and staff, especially in London and the US
Head office teams in Solihull and the US
businessModel.unitEconomics: On a £50 pair of leggings sold online, Gymshark keeps about £30 in gross margin, since gross margins for direct-to-customer apparel are often around 60%. Shipping, packing and payment cost about £5 to £7. Marketing, mainly creator fees and events, adds several pounds per order. Returns of wrong sizes eat into the rest. In stores, gross margin is similar, but rent and staff costs are higher, which is why profit has fallen while revenue grew.

howTheyGetUsers: Gymshark Athletes and other fitness creators on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok
Collection drops that trend on social media
Community events like runs, lifting meet-ups and store openings
Stores in high-traffic places like Regent Street
whatBringsUsersBack: New drops and colours every few weeks
Email and app alerts for launches
Feeling part of a fitness community
growth.moat: Gymshark's real advantage is its community. It has years of relationships with fitness creators, and many young gym-goers grew up seeing it as 'their' brand. That trust is hard to buy. But clothes are easy to copy, and rivals like Alphalete and Lululemon also use creators, so the moat depends on staying culturally relevant.

improvementIdeas.idea: Restock alerts with 'notify me' and reserved stock for app users.
improvementIdeas.problem: Sizes sell out at drops, frustrating loyal fans.

improvementIdeas.problem: Quality complaints about bobbling and see-through fabric.

improvementIdeas.problem: The app and shop feel separate.

improvementIdeas.problem: Stores are costly; they must bring in loyal customers.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Higher store sales and repeat visits.

pmLessons: Community can be a growth engine. Gymshark grew through creators rather than ads.
Direct-to-customer keeps margin and data, but fulfilment and returns are now your job.
Revenue growth is not the same as profit. New stores and markets cost money before they pay back.
Creating hype with drops works, but stockouts can frustrate the most loyal fans.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure the return on Gymshark's creator partnerships?
interviewQuestions.hint: Track sales from creator links and codes, new customer share, and cost per order. Compare with paid ads.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Gymshark open more stores?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh brand building and try-ons against rent costs. Use metrics like store payback period and online sales near stores.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature for the Gymshark Training app that drives sales.
interviewQuestions.hint: Link workouts to kit, offer rewards for streaks, early access to drops. Measure app-to-purchase conversion.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you handle quality complaints about seamless leggings?
interviewQuestions.hint: Find the root cause from reviews and returns. Fix product, communicate clearly, offer replacements. Track return rate.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow Gymshark in the US?
interviewQuestions.hint: Look at US creators, stores, delivery speed and competition. Pick a priority and define success metrics.
